Malicious URL Detection with Machine Learning¶

Step 1 — Data Collection, Preprocessing & Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Course: Computational Intelligence · Project: Malicious URL Detection using Random Forest + Ensemble Learning

This notebook turns three public URL datasets into a clean, de-duplicated, bias-corrected and leakage-free dataset with ~49 lexical features, ready for model training in Step 2.

Hard constraint from deployment: the model will run behind a FastAPI service that a Chrome extension calls for every URL the user opens. So every feature must be computable from the URL string alone (no page download, no WHOIS/DNS), and the exact same code (src/features.py) is reused by the API.

# Section What happens
1 Data Collection download + checksum verification, loading the two training sources
2 Cleaning artefact repair, garbage removal, de-duplication, data funnel
3 Normalisation / Bias fix removing the "scheme / www / path" shortcuts
4 Feature Engineering 48 lexical features, timing, NaN/inf checks
5 Splitting 70/15/15 split grouped by registered domain
6 Encoding TLD target encoding (fit on train only), label encoding of type
7 Redundancy check correlated-feature removal → final feature list
8 Scaling StandardScaler (fit on train only)
9 EDA 11 analyses with charts and insights
10 Outputs CSV / parquet / joblib / JSON files for Step 2 and the API
11 Summary key numbers

Why is Splitting (5) before Encoding (6)? The assignment lists "encode → scale → split", but the TLD encoding uses the labels (share of malicious URLs per TLD) and the scaler learns means/standard deviations. Fitting either on the full data would leak information from the test set into training. So we split first and fit both on the training split only.

All code lives in src/ (imported below); this notebook only calls it and shows the results.

1. Data Collection¶

# Dataset Origin Role
1 Malicious URLs Dataset (Kaggle, sid321axn) merged from ISCX-URL-2016, PhishTank, PhishStorm and malware-domain lists; 4 classes: benign, defacement, phishing, malware training data
2 PhiUSIIL Phishing URL Dataset (UCI #967, Prasad & Chandra, Computers & Security 2024) 235,795 URLs, mostly collected in 2023; legitimate vs phishing training data (adds recent URLs)

1.1 Loading the Kaggle file — why pd.read_csv is not enough¶

The file has two columns, url,type, but some URLs contain commas that are not quoted, and a few lines are wrapped in double quotes as a whole. A normal CSV parser then sees 3–8 columns on those lines. Let's prove it:

In [3]:
try:
    pd.read_csv(C.KAGGLE_FILE)
    print("read_csv succeeded")
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, "->", str(e)[:160])

ParserError -> Error tokenizing data. C error: Expected 2 fields in line 4028, saw 8

Fix: parse the file line by line. The label is always the last field, so url, label = line.rsplit(",", 1) is unambiguous. We strip CR/LF, surrounding quotes and whitespace, and lowercase the label (Defacement → defacement).

In [4]:

print({k: v for k, v in kinfo.items() if k != "raw_label_spellings"})
print("raw label spellings:", kinfo["raw_label_spellings"])
kaggle["type"].value_counts().rename("rows").to_frame().assign(pct=lambda d: (100 * d.rows / d.rows.sum()).round(2))

Insight: The line-by-line parser recovers all 651,097 data lines (0 lines without a comma). 903 URLs contain commas and 40 lines are wrapped in double quotes. Those are exactly the lines that break read_csv, which stops at line 4,028 because it sees 8 fields. Class mix: benign 428,101 (65.75%), defacement 96,457 (14.81%), phishing 94,019 (14.44%), malware 32,520 (4.99%). The Kaggle page states 651,191 rows, so 94 rows (0.01%) are missing from this public version. We document this as a data-quality note instead of trying to recreate rows we do not have. The labels also needed cleaning: Defacement was capitalised, and 40 labels carried a stray quote (phishing", benign").

1.2 Loading PhiUSIIL — URL and label only¶

PhiUSIIL ships 50+ pre-computed features, but we use only URL and label:

  1. Most of them come from the downloaded web page (LineOfCode, HasTitle, NoOfImage, HasPasswordField, …). Our API only sees the URL string, so it could never compute them.
  2. URLSimilarityIndex is known to be almost a copy of the label (near-leaky), and IsHTTPS is a collection artefact (see below).
  3. We want one feature definition for both sources, computed by our own code.

⚠️ In PhiUSIIL label = 1 means legitimate and 0 means phishing — the opposite of our convention — so the loader maps it explicitly.

In [5]:
phi, pinfo = D.load_phiusiil()
print({k: v for k, v in pinfo.items() if k != "columns_ignored"})
print(f"{len(pinfo['columns_ignored'])} pre-computed columns ignored, e.g.:", pinfo["columns_ignored"][:12], "...")

# Evidence for the decision: how separable are two of the ignored columns on their own?
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
pcols = pd.read_csv(C.PHIUSIIL_FILE, usecols=["URLSimilarityIndex", "IsHTTPS", "label"])
is_phish = (pcols["label"] == 0).astype(int)
evidence = pd.DataFrame({
    "legitimate (label=1)": [ (pcols.loc[pcols.label == 1, "URLSimilarityIndex"] == 100).mean() * 100,
                              pcols.loc[pcols.label == 1, "IsHTTPS"].mean() * 100 ],
    "phishing (label=0)":   [ (pcols.loc[pcols.label == 0, "URLSimilarityIndex"] == 100).mean() * 100,
                              pcols.loc[pcols.label == 0, "IsHTTPS"].mean() * 100 ],
    "single-column ROC-AUC for phishing": [ roc_auc_score(is_phish, -pcols["URLSimilarityIndex"]),
                                            roc_auc_score(is_phish, -pcols["IsHTTPS"]) ],
}, index=["% URLSimilarityIndex == 100", "% IsHTTPS == 1"]).round(3)
evidence

{'n_columns_in_file': 56, 'rows': 235795, 'raw_label_counts': {0: 100945, 1: 134850}, 'missing_url': 0, 'missing_label': 0}
54 pre-computed columns ignored, e.g.: ['FILENAME', 'URLLength', 'Domain', 'DomainLength', 'IsDomainIP', 'TLD', 'URLSimilarityIndex', 'CharContinuationRate', 'TLDLegitimateProb', 'URLCharProb', 'TLDLength', 'NoOfSubDomain'] ...
Out[5]:
legitimate (label=1) phishing (label=0) single-column ROC-AUC for phishing
% URLSimilarityIndex == 100 100.0 0.779 0.996
% IsHTTPS == 1 100.0 49.224 0.754

Insight: PhiUSIIL loads cleanly: 235,795 rows, 134,850 legitimate and 100,945 phishing, with no missing URL or label. Two of the 54 ignored columns show why we do not trust them. URLSimilarityIndex is exactly 100 for 100% of legitimate URLs but only 0.78% of phishing URLs, so on its own it separates the classes with ROC-AUC 0.996; it is close to a copy of the label. IsHTTPS is 1 for 100% of legitimate URLs versus 49.2% of phishing URLs, because the legitimate list was collected as https homepages. That is the same kind of collection artefact we remove in section 3.

1.3 Unified schema + missing values¶

Both sources are mapped to one schema:

column meaning
url_original the URL as stored in the source file
type benign / defacement / phishing / malware
label 0 = benign, 1 = malicious (phishing + malware + defacement)
source kaggle_malicious_phish or phiusiil

2. Cleaning¶

The cleaning pipeline (src/data.py::clean) runs these stages and records the row count after each one (the data funnel):

  1. Repair scraping artefacts (rows are kept, the string is fixed). While exploring the raw file we found four encoding artefacts that a browser would never send, and that are unevenly spread across classes, so a model could use them as shortcuts: '...' wrapping quotes, HTML-escaped &amp;, octal byte escapes like \321, and \%20.
  2. Drop empty / whitespace-only URLs.
  3. Drop non-printable / garbage URLs (control characters, U+FFFD replacement characters).
  4. Drop URLs longer than 2,000 characters (practical browser/server limit; extreme outliers).
  5. Drop rows whose host cannot be parsed (no host, invalid characters, no dot, no public suffix).
  6. De-duplicate on the normalised URL (section 3 explains normalisation). If one normalised URL has conflicting labels we drop all copies instead of guessing.
  7. Drop remaining duplicates within each source, then across sources (keeping the Kaggle copy).
In [7]:
t0 = time.perf_counter()
clean, funnel, det = D.clean(raw)
print(f"cleaning took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

2.1 Artefact repairs (rows changed per class)¶

In [8]:
det["repairs"]
Out[8]:
type benign defacement phishing malware total why
wrapping_single_quotes 3565 0 336 0 3901 URL wrapped in '...' (export artefact)
html_escaped_ampersand 7123 0 4122 5 11250 '&amp;' is HTML escaping; a browser sends '&'
octal_byte_escapes 0 386 0 0 386 UTF-8 bytes written as octal '\321' -> standard '%D1'
backslash_percent 3227 0 179 0 3406 '\%20' escaped percent -> '%20'

Insight: 13,312 URLs (1.5%) carried scraping artefacts, and they are not spread evenly across classes. HTML-escaped &amp; appears in 7,123 benign and 4,122 phishing URLs but in 0 defacement URLs. The escaped \% occurs in 3,227 benign versus 179 phishing URLs. Octal escapes exist only in defacement URLs (386). Left alone, a model could learn "contains amp;" or "contains a backslash" as a class signal that a real browser URL never has. After the repair, each string is what a browser would actually send.

Insight: Only 60 rows are dropped as unusable:

  • 40 non-printable URLs. Most are mojibake: Cyrillic page names decoded as Thai characters (24 of them defacement on rus-master.com).
  • 10 URLs longer than 2,000 characters (8 phishing, 2 benign).
  • 10 rows whose host cannot be parsed:
    • 5 malware "URLs" that are the dataset's own redaction placeholders (c...content-available-to-author-only...e.org);
    • 3 relative paths with no host (bin/webscr?cmd=_login-);
    • 2 hosts on the retired .an TLD.

Issue found and fixed: the first version of the host rule also dropped 175 legitimate URLs whose host is itself a public suffix (www.gov.uk, www.nhs.uk, ne.jp). We noticed this when inspecting the dropped examples, and changed the rule so these URLs are kept.

cross-source duplicates by type: {'benign': 1166, 'phishing': 52}

Insight: De-duplication is the biggest cleaning step. 4,194 normalised URLs had conflicting labels, and all 8,977 of their rows were dropped.

  • 4,132 of these conflicts are inside Kaggle. In each case a phishing copy written with http:// sits next to a benign copy written without a scheme. Example: 0000502.rcomhost.com/.../ebaymotors/pages/SignIn.php is labelled phishing with http:// and benign without it. Only 6 conflicts are byte-identical strings.
  • This is direct evidence that in the raw data the label partly depends on how the URL was written, which is exactly the shortcut section 3 removes.
  • Within each source, 20,037 duplicate rows were dropped. 11,948 were exact copies, mostly Kaggle malware (8,875) and defacement (1,149). The other 8,089 became duplicates only after normalisation; for example, 3,790 PhiUSIIL phishing URLs were listed both as http:// and https://.
  • 1,218 URLs appeared in both sources (1,166 benign, 52 phishing), and we kept the Kaggle copy.

Insight: After cleaning, 856,600 URLs remain (96.6% of the raw 886,892). Kaggle contributes 626,428 (67.1% benign, 15.2% defacement, 13.9% phishing, 3.8% malware) and PhiUSIIL 230,172 (58.1% benign, 41.9% phishing). The binary target is 554,078 benign vs 302,522 malicious (64.7% / 35.3%, ratio 1.83 : 1). That is imbalanced but not extreme, so we keep every row and compare class_weight="balanced" against no weighting in Step 2 instead of resampling now. Malware is the smallest class (23,580 URLs, 2.8% of all rows), so its recall will need watching.

3. Normalisation and the bias ("shortcut") fix¶

The problem¶

How a URL is written in our data depends on which list it came from, not on whether it is malicious:

  • Kaggle's benign URLs were mostly stored without http(s):// and without www., while its defacement and malware URLs almost always have a scheme, and many phishing URLs have www..
  • PhiUSIIL's legitimate URLs are all bare https:// homepages without a path, while many phishing URLs have a path.

A model trained on this would learn "has a scheme / has www → malicious" and "has a path → malicious". But Chrome always sends full URLs such as https://www.google.com/search?q=x, so such a model would flag Google on demo day.

The fix — src/features.py::normalize_url()¶

  1. strip whitespace, drop the #fragment
  2. remove any xxx:// scheme prefix
  3. lowercase the host (but not the path — paths can be case-sensitive)
  4. remove a leading www. / www2. … (but never the last real label: www.com stays)
  5. remove the trailing /
  6. keep port, path and query

and no feature is ever created for scheme, https or www. All features (section 4) are computed on the normalised URL.

In [12]:

3.1 Proof: shortcut rates per class before vs after normalisation (EDA 2)¶

For each source × class we measure how often the URL starts with a scheme, has a host starting with www., or contains www. anywhere. We also compute the ROC-AUC of a one-rule classifier that predicts "malicious" from that single flag (0.5 = useless, 1.0 = perfect): a high AUC before normalisation means the flag is a shortcut.

In [13]:
SCHEME = r"^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9+.\-]*://"
WWW_HOST = r"^(?:[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9+.\-]*://)?(?:[^/?#@]*@)?www\d*\."

})
flag_cols = [c for c in b.columns if c.endswith(("_before", "_after"))]

Insight: Before normalisation, the scheme alone is a strong shortcut. It is present in 100% of Kaggle defacement and 94.9% of Kaggle malware URLs but only 8.3% of Kaggle benign URLs, and a one-flag classifier reaches ROC-AUC 0.788 on Kaggle. These rates are measured on the cleaned rows; in the raw file malware is 96.3%. A host starting with www. covers 69.6% of defacement, 40.5% of phishing and 3.0% of benign URLs (AUC 0.734).

In PhiUSIIL the shortcut points the other way: 100% of legitimate URLs start with https://www.. Its www-flag AUC of 0.210 means "www → benign" works almost as well, just in reverse.

After normalisation every rate is 0.0% and every one-flag AUC is exactly 0.500, so the model can no longer see how a URL was written. www. survives only inside a few paths or queries (≤ 0.5%, e.g. embedded redirect targets). That is real content, and the embedded_url feature captures it.

3.2 The "has a path" shortcut — per source vs merged¶

Normalisation cannot remove a path (it is real information), but merging the two sources cancels the shortcut: PhiUSIIL's legitimate URLs never have a path, whereas Kaggle's benign URLs usually do.

Insight: Having a path is a shortcut only inside PhiUSIIL: 0% of its legitimate URLs have one, versus 26.8% of its phishing URLs (AUC 0.634). Inside Kaggle the shortcut does not exist (87.7% vs 88.2%, AUC 0.503) because Kaggle's benign URLs are deep links. After merging, the rates are 66.5% (benign) vs 68.6% (malicious) and the AUC drops to 0.510, so "has a path" on its own is almost useless. That is what we want, because a Google search URL has a path too. The demo table confirms that https://www.google.com/search?q=x and google.com/search?q=x now produce identical feature values.

4. Feature Engineering¶

src/features.py computes 48 lexical features per URL plus 1 encoded feature (tld_malicious_rate, section 6). Design rules:

  • pure functions, no network: tldextract.TLDExtract(suffix_list_urls=(), cache_dir=None) uses the Public Suffix List bundled inside the package;
  • computed on the normalised URL; never crashes on garbage input (IPv6, ports, user:pass@host, unicode, punycode, missing host → tested in tests/test_features.py);
  • extract_features(url) (one URL, used by the API) and extract_features_batch(series) use the same per-URL function, so training and serving can never disagree.

feature group what it measures why it can signal maliciousness
url_len length characters in the normalised URL phishing URLs pad the URL to hide the real domain
host_len length characters in the host name long hosts stack fake subdomains (paypal.com.x.y.tk)
path_len length characters in the path deep or random paths are typical of compromised sites / kits
query_len length characters in the query string long queries carry tracking ids, redirects or encoded payloads
registered_domain_len length length of the registered domain (example.co.uk) throw-away domains are often long or random
tld_len length length of the public suffix new gTLDs (.online, .support) are longer than .com / .in
num_dots count '.' in URL many dots = many subdomains or file-like names
num_hyphens count '-' in URL hyphenated look-alike domains (secure-paypal-login)
num_underscores count '_' in URL unusual in hosts; common in kit file names
num_slashes count '/' in URL path depth
num_question_marks count '?' in URL more than one '?' hints at an embedded URL
num_equals count '=' in URL number of parameter assignments
num_ampersands count '&' in URL number of extra parameters
num_at count '@' in URL '@' makes browsers ignore everything before it
num_percent count '%' in URL percent-encoding is used to obfuscate
num_tilde count '~' in URL user home directories on shared hosting
num_digits count digits in URL random ids, IPs, generated names
num_letters count letters in URL size of the alphabetic part
num_other_special count other non-alphanumeric chars (; , + ! * ...) rare in normal URLs, common in obfuscation
num_query_params count parameters in the query phishing kits pass victim data in parameters
num_path_segments count non-empty '/'-separated path parts path depth
host_num_dots count '.' in host subdomain depth
host_num_hyphens count '-' in host look-alike hosts
host_num_digits count digits in host generated / random hosts
digit_ratio statistic digits / URL length machine-generated URLs are digit-heavy
letter_ratio statistic letters / URL length human-readable URLs are letter-heavy
special_char_ratio statistic non-alphanumeric chars / URL length obfuscation and long queries
url_entropy statistic Shannon entropy of the URL (bits/char) random strings have high entropy
host_entropy statistic Shannon entropy of the host algorithmically generated domains (DGA)
longest_token_len statistic longest alphanumeric token long random tokens / hashes
avg_token_len statistic mean alphanumeric token length natural words are short
max_consecutive_repeated_char statistic longest run of one repeated character padding tricks (----, 0000)
host_vowel_ratio statistic vowels / letters in host random hosts have unnatural vowel ratios
num_subdomains host labels before the registered domain (www removed) brand names hidden in subdomains
has_ip_host host host is an IPv4 (dotted/hex/decimal) or IPv6 address no domain name = no accountability
has_port host explicit port number non-standard ports are rare for real sites
has_punycode host host contains 'xn--' (internationalised) homograph attacks (pаypal with Cyrillic a)
has_at_symbol host '@' present user-info trick http://paypal.com@evil.net
tld_in_subdomain host a label like com/net/org inside the subdomain paypal.com.evil.tk pattern
double_slash_in_path host '//' inside the path open-redirect style URLs
embedded_url host http(s): or www. inside path/query redirect chains to another site
suspicious_keyword_count lexical occurrences of words like login, verify, account social-engineering vocabulary
brand_in_non_registered_part lexical a well-known brand in subdomain/path while the domain is not that brand impersonation (apple.id-verify.xyz/apple)
is_shortener lexical domain is a URL shortener hides the real destination
suspicious_tld lexical TLD on a published most-abused list cheap / free TLDs are used for throw-away domains
risky_file_extension lexical path ends in .exe .apk .zip .js ... direct malware download
has_php lexical '.php' in path phishing kits / compromised CMS pages are mostly PHP
has_html lexical '.htm(l)' in path static phishing pages
tld_malicious_rate encoded smoothed share of malicious URLs with this TLD (train only) data-driven TLD reputation

API path == batch path on 5,000 random URLs ✔

5. Train / Validation / Test split — grouped by registered domain¶

Why grouping matters. Many URLs share a registered domain (e.g. thousands of pages of the same defaced website). With a random split, pages of the same site land in train and test, the model memorises the domain, and the test score is inflated — it would not tell us how the model does on new sites, which is exactly what the Chrome extension will see.

How. StratifiedGroupKFold (20 folds, random_state=42) never splits a group and keeps the source × type mix balanced; 14 folds → train (70%), 3 → validation (15%), 3 → test (15%). For IP-address hosts (no registered domain) the IP itself is the group.

Insight: Kaggle's labels are noisy in both directions.

  • Legitimate pages labelled phishing. The phishing class contains clearly legitimate pages: 3,212 ietf.org pages (e.g. tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1951), 548 Wikipedia articles and 685 Yahoo Groups pages. In total, 7,172 Kaggle phishing URLs (8.2%) sit on domains that also have at least 100 benign URLs. Not all of these are noise: free hosting such as angelfire.com, tripod.com and sharepoint.com really is abused by phishers. The ietf.org and Wikipedia pages, however, clearly are noise.
  • Phishing URLs labelled benign. 5,739 Kaggle URLs labelled benign contain webscr, PayPal's login-script name and a classic phishing-kit path (e.g. paypal.com.cgi.bin.webscr.cmd.login.submit....mediareso.com/...). Only 90 Kaggle phishing URLs contain it.

We do not relabel these by hand, because that would be guessing. Instead we:

  1. document them here;
  2. rely on the grouped split, so a noisy domain cannot be memorised across splits;
  3. will check them explicitly in the Step 2/3 error analysis.

This noise also lowers any accuracy we can measure on Kaggle-derived test data.

6. Encoding categorical variables¶

Our only input categorical variable is the TLD (com, co.uk, tk, …; IP hosts get the pseudo-TLD <ip>). There are hundreds of TLDs, so one-hot encoding would create hundreds of sparse columns. Instead we use target encoding with m-estimate smoothing (m = 50):

$$\text{tld\_malicious\_rate}(t) = \frac{n_{\text{malicious}}(t) + m \cdot p}{n(t) + m}$$

where $p$ is the malicious share of the training set. A TLD seen only 3 times is pulled strongly towards $p$; a TLD seen 50,000 times keeps its own rate. Unseen TLDs get $p$.

  • fitted on the training split only (UrlFeatureExtractor.fit);
  • for training rows we use out-of-fold encoding (5-fold, grouped by domain): each row is encoded with rates computed without its own fold, so its own label never leaks into its feature;
  • validation / test / the API use the full training mapping (transform).

source is not a feature (it would be a pure shortcut) and type is the target; it is label-encoded only for an optional multi-class view in Step 2.

Insight: The training prior is p = 0.3563 and 1,386 TLDs are learned.

  • For large TLDs the smoothing changes almost nothing (.com: raw 0.2482 → smoothed 0.2482; .de: 0.7544 → 0.7528).
  • TLDs seen only once are pulled strongly towards the prior: a TLD seen once, and malicious that one time, gets 0.369 instead of 1.0. That is exactly the protection against noisy rare categories we want.
  • Only 211 validation rows and 214 test rows (0.16%) have a TLD never seen in training, and these receive the prior.
  • The saved extractor reproduces the notebook features exactly from raw validation URLs, so the API will compute identical values.

type is label-encoded alphabetically: benign 0, defacement 1, malware 2, phishing 3.

7. Redundancy check → final feature list¶

Some features are almost copies of each other (e.g. num_at and has_at_symbol). Redundant features add nothing for tree models and make linear models unstable. Rule (computed on the training split only):

  1. compute the Pearson correlation of every feature pair;
  2. for every pair with |r| > 0.9 (strongest first), drop the feature with the lower mutual information with the label (MI on a 100k stratified training sample, see EDA 9).
In [26]:
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

cands = list(F.LEXICAL_FEATURES) + list(F.ENCODED_FEATURES)
Xtr = X.loc[tr, cands]
corr = Xtr.corr()
pairs = (corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape, dtype=bool), k=1)).stack()
         .rename("r").reset_index().rename(columns={"level_0": "feature_a", "level_1": "feature_b"}))
high = pairs[pairs["r"].abs() > 0.9].assign(abs_r=lambda d: d.r.abs()).sort_values("abs_r", ascending=False)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
idx_s, _ = train_test_split(np.flatnonzero(tr), train_size=100_000, stratify=clean.loc[tr, "type"], random_state=C.RANDOM_STATE)
Xs, ys = X.iloc[idx_s][cands], y[idx_s]
mi = pd.Series(mutual_info_classif(Xs, ys, discrete_features=[c in F.BINARY_FEATURES for c in cands],
                                   random_state=C.RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1), index=cands).sort_values(ascending=False)
pb = Xtr.corrwith(pd.Series(y[tr], index=Xtr.index)).fillna(0.0)   # point-biserial r
print(f"mutual information on {len(idx_s):,} rows took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

dropped, reasons = [], []
for _, rrow in high.iterrows():
    a, bb = rrow.feature_a, rrow.feature_b
    if a in dropped or bb in dropped:
        continue
    lose, keep = (a, bb) if mi[a] < mi[bb] else (bb, a)
    dropped.append(lose)
    reasons.append({"dropped": lose, "kept": keep, "r": round(rrow.r, 3), "MI dropped": round(mi[lose], 4), "MI kept": round(mi[keep], 4)})
high_tbl = high.assign(**{"MI a": high.feature_a.map(mi).round(4), "MI b": high.feature_b.map(mi).round(4)}).drop(columns="abs_r").round(3)
display(high_tbl)
decision = pd.DataFrame(reasons)
display(decision)
FINAL_FEATURES = [c for c in cands if c not in dropped]
remaining = corr.loc[FINAL_FEATURES, FINAL_FEATURES].where(~np.eye(len(FINAL_FEATURES), dtype=bool)).abs().max().max()
print(f"final feature count: {len(FINAL_FEATURES)} (dropped {len(dropped)}); max |r| left = {remaining:.3f}")
assert remaining <= 0.9
fx.feature_names = FINAL_FEATURES

Insight: 7 feature pairs exceed |r| = 0.9, and 6 features are dropped:

  • num_equals and num_ampersands: near-duplicates of num_query_params (r = 0.987 and 0.971);
  • num_path_segments: near-duplicate of num_slashes (r = 0.962);
  • num_letters: near-duplicate of url_len (r = 0.961);
  • digit_ratio: mirror image of letter_ratio (r = -0.943);
  • num_subdomains: near-duplicate of host_num_dots (r = 0.924).

In each pair we kept the feature with the higher mutual information. Its twin stays, so the information is not lost. The final model input has 43 features, and the largest remaining |r| is 0.860.

8. Scaling numerical features¶

StandardScaler rescales each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, fitted on the training split only and saved to models/scaler.joblib.

  • Tree models (Decision Tree, Random Forest, Extra Trees, boosting) split on thresholds and do not need scaling — Step 2 trains them on the raw features.
  • Distance / gradient based models (Logistic Regression, KNN, Naive Bayes) are sensitive to feature scale (url_len ranges up to 2,000 while ratios are 0–1). In Step 2 they will use the scaler inside a scikit-learn Pipeline, so cross-validation refits it per fold.
  • The parquet files keep the unscaled values; the scaler is applied at training time.
In [27]:

Validation features are close to 0 and 1 but not exactly (url_len: mean 0.018, std 0.976; has_ip_host: mean -0.072, std 0.678). That small gap is expected; it shows no validation information leaked into the scaler. Counts are heavy-tailed (a URL can be up to 1,770 characters long while the mean is about 47), so for the linear models in Step 2 we may also try a log1p transform. The class imbalance is moderate and similar in every split: 1.81 : 1 (train), 1.84 : 1 (val), 1.94 : 1 (test).

query_len 50% 0.0 20.0 0.0 0.0
url_len 75% 58.0 96.0 39.0 40.0
host_len 75% 19.0 20.0 24.0 15.0

query_len 75% 0.0 60.0 0.0 0.0
url_len mean 46.2 76.5 35.8 38.0
host_len mean 16.3 16.1 20.2 14.4
path_len mean 23.6 23.1 11.8 19.0
query_len mean 6.1 36.7 3.8 2.9

Insight: Defacement URLs are clearly the longest: median 71 characters, versus 35 (benign), 27 (phishing) and 27 (malware). They carry long CMS query strings, with a median query length of 20, while every other class has a median of 0.

After normalisation, phishing URLs are not longer than benign ones (median 27 vs 35), because Kaggle's benign class is dominated by deep article links.

Phishing has the longest hosts (median 17, 75th percentile 24, versus 15 and 19 for benign), consistent with stacked fake subdomains. Malware has the shortest hosts (median 13) because many malware URLs are bare IP addresses.

So length alone separates defacement but not phishing; it has to be combined with other features.

Insight: The TLD is the single most informative part of the URL. .com holds 57.0% of training URLs, and the top 20 TLDs together hold 87.1%. .com has a 25% malicious rate, below the 35.6% average.

Among the 101 TLDs with at least 200 training URLs:

  • 99–100% malicious: the Freenom TLDs .cf .ml .gq .ga, cheap gTLDs such as .top, .xyz, .link, .work, and IP-address hosts (<ip>, 10,205 URLs). .app is 98% malicious because of Firebase / web.app hosting of 2023 phishing.
  • Almost always benign: government and Canadian TLDs (.gov.uk 2%, .gc.ca 2%, .qc.ca 1%).

The cited suspicious_tld list matches the data: 93.8% of the 7,024 listed URLs are malicious, versus 34.9% of the rest.

Caveat: some rates reflect which list collected the data rather than real-world risk (e.g. .de 75% and .nl 80%, driven by defaced European CMS sites). That is one reason we smooth the encoding, and why we will test on fresh OpenPhish URLs.

Insight: Malware stands out on its characters: median digit ratio 0.395 (vs 0.000 for benign and phishing) and special-character ratio 0.200. Malware URLs are often IP:port download paths, e.g. Mozi botnet files such as .../Mozi.m. 3,400 training malware URLs contain mozi.

Entropy:

  • Malware hosts have the lowest host entropy (median 2.82 bits/char: only digits and dots of IP addresses).
  • Phishing hosts have the highest (3.46), matching random-looking or stacked subdomains.
  • Defacement has the highest URL entropy (4.41) because of long mixed query strings.

Structure: phishing is the only class whose box reaches one subdomain (75th percentile = 1), and it has the fewest path segments (median 0), because PhiUSIIL phishing URLs are mostly bare hosts.

No single feature separates all classes. That is the motivation for tree ensembles, which combine many weak signals.

  • risky file extension: 82.5% (n = 2,544)

They are rare (each is set on at most 1.7% of URLs), so they will help precision on a small part of the data rather than overall recall. has_php is common (10.2% of URLs) and 70.0% malicious, largely because of PHP-based defacement and phishing kits.

Surprisingly weak: brand_in_non_registered_part (41.8% malicious) and tld_in_subdomain (40.3%) are only slightly above the 35.6% average, and embedded_url (31.0%) is below it. The Kaggle benign class contains news URLs mentioning brands, share/redirect links, and the mislabelled PayPal phishing URLs from 5.0, which carry exactly these patterns.

Insight: Keywords are weaker than expected.

  • Strongly malicious: wallet (19.0×), invoice (15.6×), verify (10.3×), sign-in (6.6×) and signin (4.4×) are much more frequent in malicious URLs.
  • Not malicious at all: the most common keyword, login, is slightly more frequent in benign URLs (2.51% vs 2.08%). secure, confirm and banking are equally common in both classes.
  • Reversed by label noise: webscr, a classic PayPal phishing-kit path, is 30× more common in benign URLs (1.09% vs 0.04%), a direct symptom of the noise found in 5.0.

The malicious share by number of keyword hits is 35.2% (0 hits), 48.1% (1 hit), 33.8% (2 hits) and 29.6% (3 or more hits). The count is not monotonic, so it should be one weak feature among many, not a rule.

The point-biserial correlation adds the direction:

  • towards malicious: has_php (about +0.24), the query-parameter counts, has_ip_host and host_num_hyphens;
  • towards benign: host_vowel_ratio (-0.14), path_len (-0.14) and letter_ratio (-0.12).

All individual values are modest (MI ≤ 0.13), so no single feature solves the task. That is what we want after removing the shortcuts, and it is what makes ensembles worthwhile.

  • free hosting and app platforms: firebaseapp, weeblysite, repl, godaddysites, pantheonsite, ipfs gateways;
  • IoT-botnet malware names: mozi, sbidiot;
  • Apple-ID lures: appleid, myappleid;
  • Joomla event pages of defaced sites: jevents, listevents.

Benign-leaning tokens are mainstream sites from the Kaggle crawl era: imdb, espn, pipl, spokeo, baseball, celebrities, and torrent sites such as kickass and extratorrent. ietf appearing as a top malicious token is the label noise from 5.0 again.

Many of these tokens are domain names, which is exactly why the grouped split matters: a model that memorises firebaseapp scores well only on domains it has already seen. By raw frequency, index, php, option, itemid, view, content, article and component dominate malicious URLs. All of them are Joomla vocabulary from defacement.

EDA 11 — Defacement deep-dive¶

Defacement URLs are pages of legitimate websites that were hacked and had their content replaced. They are a special class: the URL itself was not crafted by an attacker. What do they look like?

In [38]:
patterns = {"index.php": r"index\.php", "option=com_": r"option=com_", "itemid=": r"itemid=",
            "view=article": r"view=article", "task=": r"task=", ".php?": r"\.php\?", "has a query": r"\?"}
low = T["url_normalized"].str.lower()
pat = pd.DataFrame({name: low.str.contains(rx, regex=True) for name, rx in patterns.items()})

deface_dom = T.loc[T.type == "defacement"].groupby("registered_domain").size().sort_values(ascending=False)

ax = axes[0]; x = np.arange(len(pat_rate)); w = 0.2

ax.set_xticks(x, pat_rate.index, fontsize=8.5); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter())

Insight: Defacement URLs are pages of real websites that were hacked: the URL itself was not crafted by an attacker. They look very different from the other classes:

  • 52.0% contain index.php, 41.3% the Joomla marker option=com_, 35.2% itemid= and 21.2% view=article. No other class reaches more than 1.6% on any of these patterns.
  • 56.8% have a query string, versus 13.4% of benign URLs.
  • They come from few sites: 1,486 domains for 66,700 training URLs, a median of 37 URLs per domain. Many domains contribute exactly 102 URLs, which looks like a crawl cap.

This has two consequences:

  1. Without the grouped split, the model would memorise these ~1.5k sites.
  2. The model will learn "Joomla-style query = malicious", which can cause false positives on legitimate Joomla sites. We will check this explicitly in the Step 3 error analysis.

Insight: * Data: starting from 886,892 raw URLs, we produced 856,600 clean, de-duplicated URLs (554,078 benign, 302,522 malicious; ratio 1.83 : 1).

  • Bias fix: normalisation removed the scheme/www shortcut (one-flag AUC 0.788 → 0.500), and merging the two sources removed the path shortcut (AUC 0.634 → 0.510).
  • Features: we engineered 48 lexical features plus a smoothed TLD target encoding, then dropped 6 redundant ones. That leaves 43 features in a fixed order (data/processed/feature_list.json).
  • Split: 69/15/15 by registered domain, with zero domain overlap. The TLD encoder and the scaler were fit on train only and saved for the API.

Open issues for Step 2:

  1. Label noise in Kaggle: ietf.org and Wikipedia pages labelled phishing, and PayPal phishing URLs labelled benign.
  2. Defacement URLs that look like normal CMS pages.
  3. A malware class of only 2.8%.
  4. The need to confirm on the fresh OpenPhish snapshot that the model generalises beyond the 2016–2023 data.
